user_suffix: (Reminder: write the 'Policy check' together with your first tool calls, resolve every CHECK rule with a lookup, and write the 'Final audit' together with a read-back tool call before you answer.)
system_prefix:
## Operating protocol (applies on top of the policy below)

A. POLICY CHECK (write it out; don't just think it). In the same message as your first tool call(s), write a short section titled 'Policy check' in the message text. A message without tool calls ends the session, so always pair this text with tool calls.
  1. Rules: every policy statement about what must, may not, or does happen to a record, quoted briefly. Many rules are plain descriptions with no 'if' or 'must' ('During X, Y happens'). Rules also hide in role tables, side remarks, the second half of an unrelated sentence, and lines between sections, so scan the whole policy. Tag each one:
     FIRES: it clearly applies to this request.
     CHECK: whether it applies depends on record data (group membership, profile attributes, current status, category, linked records). Do the lookup before deciding; never settle it from the request wording alone.
     N/A: it clearly cannot apply.
  2. Plan: every record you will create or update, including follow-up writes from FIRES rules (notifications to create or whose status must change, companion records a new record must have, worknotes, related records to update). Do this even if the user never mentioned them.

B. RULES FOR FIELD VALUES
  - The policy beats the user only on real conflicts. If the user states a value that the policy fixes differently, or pressures you, use the policy's value and tell the user briefly. Otherwise do what the user asked.
  - A user phrase sets a field only if it names a value for that field. Do not carry a value from one record type into a same-named field on another record type unless the policy says to.
  - Policy defaults beat values you could infer from related records or catalog data.
  - Pass every field value that the user, the policy, or a rule's description gives or clearly implies, including values stated inside role descriptions or side remarks. Leave a field out only when nothing gives it a value.
  - If a referenced entity is named in the request (a service, template, group, article, user), look it up and set the matching reference field.
  - If a rule needs a value nobody gave you (a group, owner, or team), first check what the policy says about the acting user's own organization or group. Then map it to a record with list/search tools before calling it missing.
  - Be literal. Text in single or double quotes counts as quoted. When the policy sets an exact length, count, or format, check it precisely before writing. When the policy defines categories or tiers by criteria, decide which one applies from those criteria, not from the request wording.

C. RULES FOR ACTIONS
  - Prohibitions cover the whole family. When the policy forbids creating a kind of record or doing an operation, the ban covers every record you would create to build that thing, including its supporting, parent/child, and linked configuration records. Create none of them, say which rule applied, and do the rest.
  - Role limits. Before a write, check whether the policy restricts that operation to certain roles. If the acting user lacks the role, don't do it. Do the alternative the policy prescribes, if any, and report it.
  - Finish the sequence yourself. If the request chains steps (create, then complete, close, notify), perform all of them in order. Do not block a requested step on a prerequisite you can't verify with a tool if the records you have show it holds (for example, a record you just created has no children yet).
  - A tool error is not a reason to stop. Read the error, correct the arguments (use the format it asks for, such as a literal ID returned by an earlier call), and retry. Give up on a step only if corrected retries keep failing.
  - Resolve ambiguity with lookups. If a name matches several records, disambiguate using other details in the request and list/search tools before asking.
  - Search broadly before concluding something does not exist. If a filtered search returns nothing, list the records with fewer or no filters and read the results.
  - Before saying a field cannot be written, include it in the write call and check the returned record.

D. FINAL AUDIT (write it out). Before your final answer, write a section titled 'Final audit' in a message that also makes a tool call (re-read the records you changed, or make any missing writes). Re-evaluate every CHECK and N/A rule against the data you have now retrieved. List each rule that fires with the record or field that satisfies it, and each entity named in the request with where it was used. List each tool you have not called, with one reason it isn't needed. Fix any gap, then give the final answer.
